claims.claim: Tauber: The Hobbit has 1,566 paragraphs; 85.8% are uniquely identifiable by their first three tokens and 98.5% by five or fewer.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Minimal Prefixes to Identify Hobbit Paragraphs' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021)

claims.claim: Tauber: in LOTR a single-sentence utterance followed by a tag ends in a comma before the closing quote; 'A,' said X, 'B.' versus 'A,' said X. 'B.' distinguish one interrupted sentence from two, and the first form is ambiguous.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Punctuation and Structure in Marking Up Direct Speech' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2019)

claims.claim: The Digital Tolkien Project reports speaker identification completed for The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion, enabling dialogue/narrative separation by speaker.
claims.source: Digital Tolkien Project, Overview and Sub-Projects

claims.claim: Tauber's Oxonmoot 2023 abstract applies Multidimensional Register Analysis across The Book of Lost Tales, The Hobbit, LOTR and The Silmarillion, asking whether the Silmarillion's elevated style appears in Elven direct speech in LOTR, noting these shifts had not previously been studied quantitatively.
claims.source: Digital Tolkien Project, 'Upcoming Talks' (2023) with Oxonmoot abstract 'Linguistic Variation in Tolkien's Writing Styles'
claims.quote: have not previously been studied quantitatively

claims.claim: Rateliff collates counts: LotR Project 481,103; an unofficial count 478,492 without appendices and 526,172 with; The Hobbit 95,356; The Silmarillion 130,115; Tolkien's own 1950 estimate was 600,000.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Just How Long is LotR Anyway? (word counts)', Sacnoth's Scriptorium (2017)

claims.claim: Livesey's corpus: The Hobbit 95,559 tokens; the two books of The Two Towers 66,374 and 64,738 tokens; 'ring' occurs 306 times in Fellowship (1.72 per thousand words), 70 in Two Towers (0.45) and 73 in Return of the King.
claims.source: Michael Livesey, 'The Ring Cycle: Journeying Through the Language of Tolkien's Third Age with Corpus Linguistics', JTR 18.1 (2023)

claims.claim: Beasley's chapter-level corpus of The Hobbit (19 chapters) and LOTR (5 prologue sections plus 61 chapters) totals 578,432 tokens.
claims.source: Michael H. Beasley, 'A Spatial Text Analysis of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-Earth' (USC senior thesis, 2019)
claims.quote: the total word count calculated, was 578,432

claims.claim: Shugar's grammatical analysis of The Hobbit's opening finds an average sentence length of 19 words, a longest sentence of 59 words, nested clauses with coordinating conjunctions and em-dash interruptions.
claims.source: Amelia Shugar, 'A Grammatical Journey down the Hobbit Hole' (2019)
claims.quote: an average sentence length of 19 words

claims.claim: Forum counting finds a 144-word sentence in the original Fall of Gondolin tale, cites an online claim that the longest LOTR sentence is 111 words, and corrects a 96-word count to 97; Tolkien's punctuation is credited with keeping such sentences readable.
claims.source: The Tolkien Forum thread 'Tolkien's Longest Sentence?' (2022)
claims.quote: one long sentence, counting at 144 words

claims.claim: Qiu extracts The Hobbit's dialogue by regex on text enclosed in double quotation marks across 19 chapters; top dialogue words are good (89), time (65), Baggins (46).
claims.source: Lilin Qiu, 'Quantifying Emotional Tone in Tolkien's The Hobbit' (arXiv 2512.10865, 2025)
claims.quote: text enclosed in double quotation marks

claims.claim: LotrProject reports The Hobbit has more unique words and a higher unique-word density than The Silmarillion and each LOTR volume (2009 HarperCollins eBooks, appendices excluded).

Krege's 2000 German retranslation deliberately re-differentiated Tolkien's registers, modernising the hobbits' speech into late-1990s German against a biblical high style for Elves and human nobility, where Carroux (1969-70) had used one unified style.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: German critics judged that Krege took too many liberties in a translator-centred approach unsuited to Tolkien, and the 2012 edition reverted the most controversial decisions.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Linguist Rainer Nagel found that Krege corrects Carroux's errors but often overshoots his target.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: Carroux treated the source with enormous respect and a unified linguistic style, and Tolkien was delighted with her work apart from the poems.
claims.source: Translating The Lord of the Rings (Wikipedia)

verdicts.trueWording: “In 98.5% of paragraphs, it takes five tokens or fewer”
verdicts.note: Page (fetched raw, HTTP 200): '1,542 out of 1,566 cases'; 'In 98.5% of paragraphs, it takes five tokens or fewer to identify the reference'; 'Even with just the initial three tokens you can get 85.8% of references unambiguously.' All three figures verbatim. Claim carried no quote field; every limb supported.

Page states the comma-inside-quotes convention with the final period omitted, then the two patterns verbatim ('if X says A, B. it is typeset ‘A,’ said X, ‘B.’ whereas if X says A. B. it is typeset ‘A,’ said X. ‘B.’'), and the ambiguity ('could mean that X said A, B. or that X said A B.'). LOTR context (Farewell to Lórien) confirmed. Note the text uses single quotation marks.

verdicts.trueWording: “Speaker identification has been completed for The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings, and The Silmarillion”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim under 'Text Annotation and Analysis → Status and Plans'. The 'enabling dialogue/narrative separation by speaker' gloss is supported in other words by the same section's annotation list, which pairs 'direct speech markup and speaker identification'.

verdicts.trueWording: “they have not previously been studied quantitatively”
verdicts.note: Oxonmoot abstract on the page names Book of Lost Tales, The Hobbit, LOTR and The Silmarillion; asks 'is the elevated style of The Silmarillion unique to that work or is it also the way the Elves speak in The Lord of the Rings?'; and names 'Multidimensional Register Analysis'. Quote appears as '…they have not previously been studied quantitatively.' Talk is upcoming (posted Jun 2023, Oxonmoot September), matching the 'planned' framing.

verdicts.trueWording: “The LotR Project: 481,103 words”; “478,492 without Appendices and 526,172 with them”
verdicts.note: All five figures on the page: 481,103; 'cf. 95.356 for THE HOBBIT and 130.115 for SILM' (European thousands separator = 95,356 and 130,115); 'In February 1950 Tolkien tells Unwin the newly finished book is 600,000 words'. The 478,492/526,172 pair appears in Rateliff's own signed comment ('the unofficial but reliable result of 478,492 without Appendices and 526, 172 with them'), not the post body. Page also records Tolkien's later 1950 escalations to 1m and 1.2m words, which the claim does not mention.

verdicts.trueWording: “books four and six… including only 66,374 and 64,738 tokens each”
verdicts.note: Landing page carries only the abstract; the full article was reached as raw PDF via Wayback (web.archive.org/web/20250602181027id_/…viewcontent.cgi?article=1327, 44pp, text extracted). Quote 'a total wordcount of 95,559 tokens' is verbatim. Ring counts verbatim: '306 times in The Fellowship (1.72/thousand words); 70 times in The Two Towers (0.45/thousand words); and 73 times in The Return of the King'. But the two sub-corpus figures are misattributed: Livesey writes 'books four and six', i.e. the second book of The Two Towers and the second book of The Return of the King — not 'the two books of The Two Towers' (which would be books three and four).
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that 66,374 and 64,738 are the two books of The Two Towers — the article says books four and six

verdicts.note: Landing page is abstract-only; full thesis reached as raw PDF via Wayback (…20240222182336id_/…viewcontent.cgi?article=1299, 77pp). Page: 'this began with one “chapter” of notes at the beginning of The Hobbit, followed by its nineteen chapters. Five “chapters” of prologue began The Lord of the Rings, with its three volumes comprising the remaining sixty-one chapters', total 86 columns; quote verbatim. The claim omits the one extra 'notes' column for The Hobbit, which the source says the 578,432 total includes.

verdicts.trueWording: “In a piece with an average sentence length of 19 words”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Also on the page: 'This 59-word sentence is the longest one within the section I analyzed'; 'propelled by the nested clauses and coordinating conjunctions'; and the em-dash interruption ('All’s right with the world and then… EM DASH… “Gandalf came by”'). Byline on the page reads 'By Amelia Turkette', March 2019, on ameliashugar.com — the attribution name differs from the byline.

verdicts.trueWording: “There is ‘information’ on the web indicating the longest sentence found to be 111 words”
verdicts.note: Live site is behind a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403 with browser UA); reached via Wayback raw capture 20260820220652id_. Quote 'one long sentence, counting at 144 words' verbatim (post #10 by Ent), about the Fall of Gondolin original tale quoted in post #1. Also verbatim: 'The one he cites at 96 words is actually 97' and 'Tolkien’s (arguably) correct use of punctuation saves the sentence so it does not grind the mind into submission.' But the 111-word figure is not tied to LOTR anywhere on the page — the thread is about Tolkien's longest sentence generally and the source sentence is from The Fall of Gondolin.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the 111-word online claim concerns The Lord of the Rings — the page says only 'the longest sentence found', naming no work

verdicts.trueWording: “Dialogue is identified by detecting text enclosed in double quotation marks”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (§2.3). Page: 'All spoken dialogue is extracted chapter by chapter using Python’s re module'; 'the nineteen chapters of The Hobbit' / 'all 19 chapters'; 'The Cirrus output shows good (89), time (65), Baggins (46), mountain (42), and Thorin (41) as the most frequently appearing dialogue words.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “The Hobbit has more unique words and a higher unique word density than both the Silmarillion and each volume in the Lord of the Rings”
verdicts.note: Live host returns a WAF block (HTTP 454); reached via Wayback raw capture 20260808182141id_. Quote 'higher unique word density' verbatim, and the appendices exclusion is on the page ('neither has the appendicies to the Lord of the Rings… since they are not part of the story'). No edition is named anywhere in the capture — 'HarperCollins', '2009' and 'edition' do not occur; a 2013 capture of the same URL also lacks them.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 2009 HarperCollins eBook editions as the source texts — no edition is named on the page

verdicts.trueWording: “modernising the language of the Hobbits into the linguistic style of late 1990s German”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the 'German (Carroux) 1969–1970' section. Page: 'In 2000, Klett-Cotta published a new translation by Wolfgang Krege… It focuses more on the differences in linguistic style that Tolkien employed to set apart the more biblical prose and the high style of elvish and human ‘nobility’ from the more colloquial 1940s English spoken by the Hobbits, something that Krege thought Carroux’s more unified version was lacking.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “critics felt that he took too many liberties”; Nagel: a “translator-centred approach”
verdicts.note: Quote 'translator-centred approach' is verbatim on the page, and 'The 2012 edition of Krege has reverted the most controversial of his decisions' supports the second half of the claim. But the page attributes the too-many-liberties judgement to unnamed 'critics' and the 'translator-centred approach' / 'style unsuitable for Tolkien' wording to one named linguist, Rainer Nagel — the claim merges the two into a single collective judgement by 'German critics'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that 'German critics' called it a translator-centred approach unsuited to Tolkien — the page attributes that phrase to the linguist Rainer Nagel alone

verdicts.trueWording: “Krege corrects many errors in Carroux, but ‘often overshoots its target of modernising’”
verdicts.note: Quote 'often overshoots its target' verbatim; Nagel is identified on the page as 'The linguist Rainer Nagel'. Two compressions, neither contradicted: the source says 'many errors in Carroux' (not all), and the target is specified as 'its target of modernising'.

verdicts.trueWording: “treating its source with ‘enormous respect’”; “Tolkien was delighted with Carroux’s work”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Page: 'Tolkien was delighted with Carroux’s work, with the sole exception of the poems and songs.' The unified-style limb is supported by 'Krege thought Carroux’s more unified version was lacking' and by the lead's 'using a similar linguistic style for the speech of both elves and hobbits'. Note 'enormous respect' is the Tolkien scholar Susanne Stopfel's characterisation, which the claim states unattributed.
